lessons.title: Close-up: the lamb and the sleeve

held.why: Only Louvre sources (the record and the 2019 exhibition guide, both from the museum's paintings department) say Anne's robe stayed at the underlayer stage; held until an independent second source places it.

zoom.label: The child Jesus gripping the lamb, lower right

c1.text: Level one: the lamb stands for the child's future sacrifice, and John once stood in its place. Leonardo didn't invent this lamb for the panel.

zoom.label: The child Jesus gripping the lamb, lower right

c1q.text: Which earlier Leonardo design already had a lamb here?

sources.title: Louvre collection record, INV 776, La Vierge, l'Enfant Jésus et sainte Anne (commentary by Vincent Delieuvin, 2021)
British Museum, 1875,0612.17, Leonardo, sketch for the Virgin and Child with St Anne (curator's comments, citing Popham & Pouncey, Italian Drawings in the British Museum, 1950)
National Gallery, London, NG6337, The Burlington House Cartoon
Louvre collection record, INV 777, La Vierge aux rochers (commentary by Vincent Delieuvin, 2021)
Colette Féraudet, 'La Vierge aux rochers', Panorama de l'art (Rmn-Grand Palais), 27 Mar 2023

c1m.text: A lamb by 1501, John in the London cartoon: which design came first is still argued.

c1a.text: Yes. A letter of April 1501 describes a Leonardo cartoon in which the child takes a lamb and seems to squeeze it.

c1b.text: That large drawing has John here, not a lamb.

correction.tempting: The London cartoon is the famous large drawing of this very group, so it looks like the obvious model.
correction.truth: In the London cartoon little John the Baptist stands where this lamb is; in the painting, the lamb takes his place.
correction.evidence: National Gallery: the lamb "appears in the place of the toddler John the Baptist".

c1c.text: Same artist, same room, but no lamb there.

correction.tempting: In the Virgin of the Rocks, hanging nearby in room 710, a second small figure faces Jesus too.
correction.truth: That figure is the infant John the Baptist, kneeling. There is no lamb in the Virgin of the Rocks.
correction.evidence: The Louvre and the Grand Palais: in the Virgin of the Rocks, Jesus blesses the kneeling infant John.

zoom.label: Mary's right arm in its transparent sleeve, from wrist to shoulder

c2.text: Mary reaches down with her right arm. Look at the cloth over it: thin, see-through folds, wrapping the arm from wrist to shoulder.

zoom.label: Mary's right arm in its transparent sleeve, from wrist to shoulder

c2q.text: How did Leonardo work out these folds?

sources.title: Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 912532, The drapery of the Madonna's arm
Louvre, Leonardo da Vinci 1452–1519 exhibition guide (English, 2019), p. 104
National Gallery, London, NG6337, The Burlington House Cartoon
British Museum, 1875,0612.17, Leonardo, sketch for the Virgin and Child with St Anne (curator's comments, citing Popham & Pouncey, Italian Drawings in the British Museum, 1950)
Smarthistory, Dr Beth Harris and Dr Steven Zucker, Leonardo, Virgin and Child with St Anne and St John the Baptist (cartoon)

c2m.text: This arm got its own study: transparent folds, wrist to shoulder. The sheet is at Windsor.

c2a.text: Yes. He drew this arm's drapery on its own sheet, now in the Royal Collection at Windsor; the Louvre showed it in 2019.

c2b.text: That drawing was never used for tracing.

correction.tempting: The London cartoon shows this same group at large scale, so tracing from it sounds efficient.
correction.truth: The London cartoon was never pricked or incised, so it wasn't used to transfer a design.
correction.evidence: National Gallery: "neither pricked nor incised to allow for the design to be transferred".

c2c.text: That sketch was for another stage of the design.

correction.tempting: Leonardo did try out this group in a quick sketch, now in the British Museum.
correction.truth: That sketch works out the London cartoon's poses, with John. This arm's folds got their own careful study.
correction.evidence: British Museum: its sketch is "very close, albeit in reverse," to the cartoon. Royal Collection: a study for the Madonna's arm.

zoom.label: Saint Anne's dress over her legs, lower left of centre

c3.text: Level one: Leonardo was still studying the folds of Anne's dress in France. Look at that dress over her legs.

zoom.label: Saint Anne's dress over her legs, lower left of centre

c3q.text: Why does Anne's dress look flatter than Mary's?

sources.title: Louvre collection record, INV 776, La Vierge, l'Enfant Jésus et sainte Anne (commentary by Vincent Delieuvin, 2021)
Louvre, Leonardo da Vinci 1452–1519 exhibition guide (English, 2019), p. 105
Gareth Harris, 'Louvre's Leonardo plan leads to resignation', The Art Newspaper, 1 Feb 2012

c3m.text: The dress stayed unfinished: the last idea never reached the panel.

c3a.text: Yes. The Louvre says this robe stayed at the underlayer stage: his last drapery idea never reached the panel.

c3b.text: Soft, yes, but not by design.

correction.tempting: Sfumato softens edges on purpose, as in the Mona Lisa.
correction.truth: Here the dress was simply never finished.
correction.evidence: The Louvre: the robe "est demeurée à l'état de sous-couche".

c3c.text: The cleaning thinned varnish, not this robe.

correction.tempting: The 2011 cleaning was criticised for possibly harming paint.
correction.truth: It thinned old varnish; the robe was never finished.
correction.evidence: The Art Newspaper: "thinning layers of 19th- and 20th-century varnish". The Louvre: the robe stayed an underlayer.

extends.concept: The lamb's meaning and the designs with John or a lamb

c1q.what_you_learn: The lamb was already in the cartoon Novellara described in 1501; the London cartoon and the Virgin of the Rocks put John beside the child instead.
